readerTitle: Your customers are happy. So why are they leaving?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, 포장재 공급업체) + 실제 연구 (Jones & Sasser, 1995 HBR)
insight: 만족은 지난 경험에 대한 평가이고, 충성은 다른 선택지가 나타났을 때 우리를 다시 고르는 미래의 행동이다. '그럭저럭 만족'은 떠날 준비가 된 상태일 수 있다.
misconception: 만족도 점수가 높으면 고객은 남는다. 불만이 없으면 충성 고객이다.

sources.text: Jones, T. O. & Sasser, W. E. (1995). Why Satisfied Customers Defect. Harvard Business Review, Nov–Dec 1995.
청소 서비스와 포장재 공급업체 사례, 점수별 재예약률 차트의 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Jones & Sasser(1995)에 나오는 Xerox 사례: '완전히 만족(totally satisfied)'한 고객이 '만족(satisfied)'한 고객보다 18개월 안에 재구매할 가능성이 약 6배 높았다는 내용. 게시 전 원문에서 배수와 기간을 다시 확인하세요.
'hostages'(전환 비용 때문에 불만족해도 머무는 고객)라는 표현이 Jones & Sasser 논문의 분류에서 왔는지 확인하세요. 카드에는 출처 없이 일반 설명으로만 썼습니다.
3번 카드 차트 수치(5점 85%, 4점 50%, 3점 40%)는 모두 가상입니다. 4점이 5점보다 3점에 더 가깝다는 점을 보여주려는 설명용 수치입니다.

cards.title: Your customers are happy. So why are they leaving?
body: For two years, the same cleaner came to your home every other Friday. Good work. No problems. If she'd sent a survey, you'd have given her 4 out of 5.
Then a neighbor mentioned someone a little cheaper. You switched that week, without much thought. You were satisfied. You just weren't loyal.

image.label: A homeowner waving goodbye to one cleaner while greeting another
image.brief: 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트. 집 현관에서 집주인이 한쪽 청소부에게 손을 흔들어 작별하고, 다른 쪽에서 새 청소부가 도착함. 떠나는 청소부 머리 위에 별 4개 평점 말풍선. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: 92% satisfied. 30% gone.
body: You run a home cleaning service. Your yearly survey says 92% of customers are satisfied or very satisfied. Yet 30% of last year's customers didn't book again.

options.text: The survey is flawed. People are just being polite
options.feedback: Politeness plays a part, but the answers can be honest. Customers really were satisfied. Satisfaction just doesn't tell you who will come back.

options.text: Satisfied isn't the same as staying. Compare who rebooked with who didn't
options.feedback: This looks at behavior instead of scores. It costs some digging, but it shows what actually makes people return.

options.text: Push satisfaction higher with free extras for everyone
options.feedback: It spends money on people who were already happy, and many were leaving anyway. More of the same won't give them a reason to stay.

cards.title: A 4 behaves more like a 3 than a 5.
body: Sorting customers by their survey score and checking who rebooked tells a clear story. The big jump isn't between unhappy and happy. It's between *fine* and *delighted*.

groups.label: Rebooked within a year, by satisfaction score

cards.title: Satisfaction looks back. Loyalty looks forward.
body: **Satisfaction** is a judgment about the past: did you get what you expected? **Loyalty** is a behavior in the future: do you choose this business again when another option shows up?
A satisfied customer has no complaint. A loyal customer has a reason to stay. Those are different things, and only the second one protects your revenue.

image.label: A rear-view mirror labeled satisfaction and a road ahead labeled loyalty
image.brief: 자동차 운전석 시점. 백미러 속에는 'Satisfaction: How was it?'라는 지나온 길, 앞 유리 너머에는 갈림길과 'Loyalty: Will they choose you again?' 표지판. 단순한 벡터 스타일.

cards.title: Researchers found the same gap.
body: In a 1995 Harvard Business Review article, "Why Satisfied Customers Defect," Thomas Jones and Earl Sasser argued that merely satisfied customers leave far more easily than most managers assume.

Their best-known example came from Xerox. Customers who said they were *totally* satisfied were about six times more likely to buy again over the next 18 months than customers who said they were just satisfied.
The lesson: a high average score can hide a large group that is only one good offer away from leaving.

cards.title: No complaint is not a reason to stay.
body: Satisfied customers leave for ordinary reasons: a cheaper offer, a friend's recommendation, a move, or simply nothing memorable to hold them.

Loyalty grows from something a rival can't easily match. That might be a person who knows your preferences, results you can't get elsewhere, or a fix that saves you real trouble. It's the gap between *good enough* and *hard to replace*.
cards.softwareNote: Users can rate an app 4 stars and still cancel when a cheaper tool appears. Track renewals, how often people come back and how much of their work runs through the product, not just survey scores.

cards.title: Don't swing too far the other way.
body: Satisfaction still matters. Unhappy customers usually leave fastest, so fixing real problems comes first.

And some customers stay without being satisfied at all, because switching is too costly or there's no alternative. That looks like loyalty in your numbers, but it isn't. When a real alternative arrives, these customers often leave all at once, and they tell others why.

cards.title: Now it's a packaging supplier.
body: You make shipping boxes for a mid-sized food producer. Every quarter they rate you "satisfied." Now their purchasing team has asked three suppliers, including you, to bid for next year's contract.
What best improves your chances of keeping them?

options.text: Trust the scores and submit your usual bid
options.feedback: It saves effort, but "satisfied" only means you met the bar. A rival who meets the same bar for less wins on price.

options.text: Cut your price to beat any likely rival
options.feedback: It may keep the contract, but it lowers your margin and teaches them you compete on price. The next bid starts lower.

options.text: Find their biggest headache, like late deliveries or storage space, and offer a fix rivals can't easily match
options.feedback: It takes time and may cost you something extra, but it gives them a reason to choose you beyond price. That is loyalty, not just satisfaction.

cards.softwareNote: Business software faces the same moment at renewal. A customer who is only satisfied compares prices; one whose team depends on your product rarely runs the comparison.

cards.title: Satisfied customers have no complaint. Loyal customers have a reason.
body: A good score tells you that you met expectations. Only behavior, like rebooking, renewing and buying more, tells you who will stay.
**Try it today:** list five customers who rated you well. Next to each, write the one thing they would lose if they switched to a rival. Blank lines are your risk.
